q: Name an eponymous law or rule of computing.

answers.l: Gordon Moore, 1965: transistor counts double regularly. He revised it to every two years in 1975.
Named for Edward Murphy, an engineer on rocket-sled tests in 1949.
Mel Conway, 1968: systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them.
Adding people to a late software project makes it later.
It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take Hofstadter’s law into account.
Be conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept. From the TCP spec.
With enough users, every observable behavior of your API will be depended on by somebody.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
Work expands to fill the time available.
The serial part caps your speedup, however many cores you add.
A network’s value grows with the square of its users.
Eighty percent of the effects from twenty percent of the causes.
Debugging is twice as hard as writing the code, so if you write it as cleverly as possible you can’t debug it.
Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow. Named by Eric Raymond.
Software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster.
Every program attempts to expand until it can read mail.
Any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains a slow, buggy half of Common Lisp. There were no rules one through nine.
Any application that can be written in JavaScript will eventually be written in JavaScript.
A complex system that works evolved from a simple system that worked.
L = λW: items in a queue equal arrival rate times time spent waiting.
The best way to get the right answer online is to post the wrong one.
Talk only to your immediate friends. Named for the Demeter project at Northeastern, 1987.
Time to hit a target depends on its size and distance. Why screen corners are prime real estate.
Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
The first 90% of the code takes 90% of the time; the other 10% takes the other 90%. Tom Cargill, Bell Labs.
Any code of your own you haven’t looked at for six months might as well have been written by someone else.
Amdahl’s optimistic sibling: bigger problems parallelize better.
Moore’s law for disk density.
Power density stays constant as transistors shrink. It broke down in the mid-2000s.
Ninety percent of everything is crud.
Any headline that ends in a question mark can be answered by the word no.
People get promoted to their level of incompetence.
Decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of choices.
Complexity can’t be removed, only moved. Larry Tesler also gave us cut, copy and paste.
Users spend most of their time on other sites, so make yours work like those.
Leading digits are mostly small. Fraud detection relies on it.
Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by stupidity.
In language design, debate grows with how superficial the feature is. Comment syntax gets the most.
1953: computer performance grows with the square of its cost.
A new class of computer appears roughly every decade.
Computations per joule doubled roughly every 1.6 years.
The cost of a chip fab doubles every four years.
GPU performance grows faster than Moore’s law.
An evolving system grows more complex unless work is done to reduce that.

nope.premature optimization: A quote, not a named law. Try the slang prompt.

traps.q: Name the law from Gordon Moore’s 1965 article about transistor counts.
Name the law that says systems mirror the organizations that build them.
